title: tfestimator does not work with distribute strategy from tensorflow v1.10 and up, return "C stack usage XX is too close to limit" error
description:
tfestimator does not appear to work with any of the DistributionStrategy that Google provides for automatic scaling of estimators to multiple GPUs.  It errors out with a "C stack usage XXXX is too close to the limit".

Minimum reproduce-able example (converted to R from:  https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/master/tensorflow/contrib/distribute/README.md)

```
library("tensorflow")
library("tfestimators")

model_fn <- function(features, labels, mode, params, config)
{
  layer   <- tf$layers$Dense(1L)
  logits  <- layer(features)
  
  if(mode == tf$estimator$ModeKeys$PREDICT) 
  {
    predictions = dict("logits", logits)
  }
  
  loss = tf$losses$mean_squared_error(labels = labels, predictions = tf$reshape(logits, list()))
  
  if(mode == tf$estimator$ModeKeys$EVAL)
  {
    return(estimator_spec(mode = mode, loss = loss))
  }
  
  if(mode == tf$estimator$ModeKey$TRAIN)
  {
    train_op = tf$train$GradientDescentOptimizer(0.2)$minimize(loss)
  }
  
  return(estimator_spec(mode = model, loss= loss, train_op = train_op))
}  


input_fn <- function()
{
  features <- tf$data$Dataset$from_tensors(list(list(1.0)))$'repeat'(100L)
  labels = tf$data$Dataset$from_tensors(1.0)$'repeat'(100L)
  
  return(tf$data$Dataset$zip(tuple(features, labels)))
}

## MAIN PROGRAM LOOP ##

distribution = tf$contrib$distribute$MirroredStrategy()
config = tf$estimator$RunConfig(train_distribute = distribution)

classifier <- estimator(model_fn, config = config)

train(classifier, input_fn)
evaluate(classifier, input_fn)

```
Error returned:

title: tfestimators linear_regressor and dnn_regressor vs lm
description:
Good afternoon,
I'm just starting to learn tfestimators. I was interested on comparing the performance of `linear_regressor()` and `dnn_regressor()` vs a "standard" `lm()`. My results, however, are very disconcerting.
I paste in here a self-contained example:

```
### testing TensorFlow estimators ----

# create data.frame data1 with response as a linear
# combination of the predictors

n.observations <- 1e3
n.predictors <- 20

x <- matrix(runif(n.observations*n.predictors,0,1),ncol=n.predictors)
w <- runif(n.predictors,-20,20) # random weights
b <- runif(1,0,1) # random bias

colnames(x) <- sprintf("x%03i",1:ncol(x))

y <- x %*% w + b
y <- jitter(y[,1],500) # add some noise

data1 <- as.data.frame(x)
data1$response <- y


library(tfestimators)

# create helper functions for tf

features <- function() colnames(x)
response <- function() "response"

feature_columns <- feature_columns(
  column_numeric(features(),shape=c(1L))
)

input_fn1 <- function(data) {
  input_fn(data, features = features(), response = response(), epoch=30)
}



# create tf classifiers: linear_regression and dnn_regression

classifier1 <- linear_regressor(
  feature_columns = feature_columns
)

classifier2 <- dnn_regressor(
  feature_columns = feature_columns,
  hidden_units = c(5,5)
)

# divide data into training and testing sets

resample <- modelr::resample_partition(data1, c(test = 0.1, train = 0.9))
data1.train <- as.data.frame(resample$train)
data1.test <- as.data.frame(resample$test)

# train models

lm0 <- lm(response ~ .,data1.train)
train(classifier1, input_fn = input_fn1(data1.train))
train(classifier2, input_fn = input_fn1(data1.train))

# predictions from models

predictions0 <- predict(lm0,newdata = data1.test)
predictions1 <- predict(classifier1, input_fn = input_fn1(data1.test))
predictions2 <- predict(classifier2, input_fn = input_fn1(data1.test))

# plot the predictions

plot.predictions <- function(predicted.values) {
  plot(x <- data1.test$response,predicted.values,
       xlab="Actual value",
       ylab="Predicted value")
  abline(0,1)

  mtext(sprintf("R2=%1.3f",cor(x,predicted.values)^2),3,-2,cex=.8)
}

par(mfrow=c(1,3),pch=19)

title("lm modeling")

plot.predictions(unlist(predictions1))
title("linear_regressor")

plot.predictions(unlist(predictions2))
title("dnn_regressor")

```
I am not sure what I am missing, but the predictions of both linear_regressor and dnn_regressor are extremely poor. I haven't been able to find an useful example to understand what is wrong in the above approach.
Thanks in adance

description:
This might be a very basic question.
I'm running the example provided in https://tensorflow.rstudio.com/tfestimators/articles/examples/iris_dnn_classifier.html

``` 
library(tfestimators)

response <- function() "Species"
features <- function() setdiff(names(iris), response())

# split into train, test datasets
set.seed(123)
partitions <- modelr::resample_partition(iris, c(test = 0.2, train = 0.8))
iris_train <- as.data.frame(partitions$train)

# construct feature columns

  column_numeric(features())
)

  feature_columns = feature_columns,
  hidden_units = c(10, 20, 10),
  n_classes = 3
)

# construct input function 
iris_input_fn <- function(data) {
  input_fn(data, features = features(), response = response())
}

# train classifier with training dataset
set.seed(123)
train(classifier, input_fn = iris_input_fn(iris_train))

# valuate with test dataset
predictions <- predict(classifier, input_fn = iris_input_fn(iris_test))
evaluation <- evaluate(classifier, input_fn = iris_input_fn(iris_test))
```
To ensure reproducibility, I added a second `set.seed(123)` right before the training.
When comparing the predictions to the actual values in the test dataset, I found that all cases in this dataset have been predicted to belong to the same class:

```
table(iris_test$Species,unlist(predictions$class_ids))
```

Returns:

```            
              2
  setosa     11
  versicolor 10
  virginica   8
```

Is this performance the expected from dnn_classifier?
Compare that to the output of a random forest classification:

```
# random forest

library(randomForest)
set.seed(123)
rforest <- randomForest(Species ~ .,iris_train)
table(iris_test$Species,predict(rforest,newdata=iris_test))
```
Returns a much better classification:

Consider the Wide & Deep Example available [here](https://tensorflow.rstudio.com/tfestimators/articles/examples/wide_and_deep.html)

title: Backward compatibility
description:
Per JJ:

Our principle is that all versions of our R wrapper packages should work with the current TF version (dev master if possible) as well as all previous versions back to some threshold. For example, the tensorflow package works on all versions of tensorflow back to v1.0 and the Keras package works on all versions of Keras from 2.0.8 all the way back to 2.0.0. If we don't do this it becomes very awkward for both devs and end users (as we are now experiencing with tfestimators).

The keras package has many examples of how to support newer versions while still not failing against older version. In your example of an argument being added, we simply switch our calling semantics to `do.call` and conditionally include the new argument. For example here (https://github.com/rstudio/keras/blob/master/R/model.R#L613-L625):

```r
predict_generator <- function(object, generator, steps, max_queue_size = 10, verbose = 0) {
  
  args <- list(
    generator = generator,
    steps = as.integer(steps),
    max_queue_size = as.integer(max_queue_size)
  )
  
  if (keras_version() >= "2.0.1")
    args$verbose <- as.integer(verbose)
  
  call_generator_function(object$predict_generator, args)
}
```

In this case I am silently ignore the argument in earlier versions. This might be okay or we depending on what the argument is you might want to checking for `!missing` and issue a warning. 

You could also have functions which bomb out entirely if the right version isn't available. The main idea is that given the way the R package system works (users tend to get forced to the latest version by CRAN + availability of bug fixes) we can't afford to tie our R package versions to the latest Python package versions.

I had assumed that the reason for our v1.3.0 branch was some fundamental incompatibility with TF v1.4. If however the only concern is new arguments or some functions that require TF v1.4 we should just add the conditional code like that above required to enable everyone to develop on and use the master branch.

title: re-visit feature columns specification?
description:
I'd like to propose a re-working of the syntax we use for feature column definitions. Currently, feature columns are defined as e.g.

```R
cols <- feature_columns(
  column_numeric(starts_with("a")),
  column_numeric("cyl")
)
```

It feels to me that we could try to express this in a more 'pattern-matching' way, e.g.

```R
cols <- feature_columns(
    starts_with("a") ~ column_numeric(dtype = tf$float32),
    "cyl"            ~ column_numeric(dtype = tf$float32)
)
```

This feels a bit cleaner as it separates the 'condition' from the 'object constructed from that condition'. We could also mix in plain, non-formula objects in the call e.g.

```R
cols <- feature_columns(
    starts_with("a") ~ column_numeric(dtype = tf$float32),
    "cyl"            ~ column_numeric(dtype = tf$float32),
    c("a1", "a2")    ~ column_crossed()
    column_numeric("other"),
)
```

What do you think @jjallaire @terrytangyuan?

description:

```r
library(dplyr)
```

```
Attaching package: ‘dplyr’

The following objects are masked from ‘package:tfestimators’:

    contains, ends_with, everything, matches, one_of, starts_with
```

Obviously once dplyr imports tidyselect and that version of dplyr is on CRAN this problem will go away, but the dev version of dplyr does not yet depend on tidyselect so it seems unlikely that this change will make it to CRAN soon.

I think we need to deal with this before publicizing tfestimators as I'm sure people will want to use the two packages together.  

Since we only use `vars_select` in a couple of places (https://github.com/rstudio/tfestimators/search?utf8=%E2%9C%93&q=vars_select&type=) it seems like one solution might be to do the evaluation of `vars_select` in a special environment that has access to the tidyselect filtering functions. title: consider re-organizing S3 class hierarchy for tfestimator objects
description:
Consider the class currently applied for e.g. the output of `linear_regressor()`:

```
> class(tf_model)
[1] "tf_model"  "linear"    "regressor"
```

I think there's a couple tweaks we could make here:

1. Should these have class `tf_estimator` rather than `tf_model`? The underlying object really is just an R object wrapping over an estimator, so it is perhaps more accurate to call it that.

2. We should also prefix the extra classes with `tf_estimator` (or `tf_model`) -- standalone S3 class names e.g. `linear` feel a bit odd to me.

E.g. for `linear_regressor()` I think the class output should be more like:

```
> class(tf_model)
[1] "tf_estimator"  "tf_estimator_regressor"    "tf_estimator_regressor_linear"
```

In other words, I think the three main things worth encoding in the class of the object are:

1. It's an estimator,
2. It's a regressor vs. it's a classifier,
3. The actual full class of the estimator.

@jjallaire @terrytangyuan, let me know if you think this sounds sensible, or if there are any other bits worth adding as a class. (For example, do you think it's necessary that we differentiate between 'canned' estimators provided by the `tfestimators` package, and user-defined estimators? It would be nice if there were effectively no difference and we didn't have to customize behaviors based on whether we defined the estimator vs. the user defined the estimator)

```
    train(input_fn = .input_fn)
```

The `tf_model` object would need to keep a reference to the (last used?) `input_fn` that was used for training. Or is this is a bit too far outside of the TensorFlow paradigm?

title: enhanced name scopes for tidyselect
description:
We current establish the name scope for tidyselect via the first argument to `feature_columns()`, e.g.

```r
fc <- feature_columns(mtcars,
  column_numeric(disp),
  column_numeric(cyl)
)
```

This works fine for simple cases, however in some cases you actually need to create named variables which map to the feature columns (so that you can create embeddings). For example, consider this code:

```r
# Categorical base columns
education <- column_categorical_with_hash_bucket("education", hash_bucket_size = 1000L, dtype = tf$int32)
relationship <- column_categorical_with_hash_bucket("relationship", hash_bucket_size = 100L, dtype = tf$int32)
workclass <- column_categorical_with_hash_bucket("workclass", hash_bucket_size = 100L, dtype = tf$int32)
occupation <- column_categorical_with_hash_bucket("occupation", hash_bucket_size = 100L, dtype = tf$int32)
native_country <- column_categorical_with_hash_bucket("native_country", hash_bucket_size = 1000L, dtype = tf$int32)

# Continuous base columns.
age <- column_numeric("age")
age_buckets <- column_bucketized(age, boundaries = list(18, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 65))
education_num <- column_numeric("education_num")
capital_gain <- column_numeric("capital_gain")
capital_loss <- column_numeric("capital_loss")
hours_per_week <- column_numeric("hours_per_week")

#' ### Define Wide and Deep Columns

wide_columns <- list(native_country, education, occupation, workclass, relationship, age_buckets)

deep_columns <- list(
  column_embedding(workclass, dimension = 8L),
  column_embedding(education, dimension = 8L),
  column_embedding(relationship, dimension = 8L),
  column_embedding(native_country, dimension = 8L),
  column_embedding(occupation, dimension = 8L),
  age, education_num, capital_gain, capital_loss, hours_per_week)

#' ### Combining Wide and Deep Models into One

model <- linear_dnn_combined_classifier(
  linear_feature_columns = wide_columns,
  dnn_feature_columns = deep_columns,
  dnn_hidden_units = c(100L, 50L)
)
```

Here we are forced back into the use of strings for referring to columns (because we need to create addressable R objects for subsequent calls to `column_embedding()`.

I think this re-raises the issue of how the current tidyselect "scope" is established. It would be very nice to be able to somehow set it globally so that instances like the above could use tidyselect as well as so that you can write arbitrary R code to build up feature columns (it seems likely that *just* relying on pattern matching won't be enough to capture all cases, especially when hyper-parameters drive which columns are included). 

A couple of possibilities:

```r
active_feature_columns(mtcars)
cyl <- column_numeric(cyl)
disp <- column_numeric(disp)
```

```r
with_columns(mtcars, {
   cyl <- column_numeric(cyl)
   disp <- column_numeric(disp)
})
```

Note that our current syntax is really just another (less flexible) way of expressing the latter (scoped availability of active feature columns):

```r
feature_columns(mtcars,
   column_numeric(cyl),
   column_numeric(disp)
)
```

Except that our current syntax is only capable of producing an R list and can't handle any imperative code.

@hadley, @terrytangyuan, and @kevinushey what do you think the of the `with_columns` syntax?

title: A better and instructive enforcement for custom model function
description:
For example, during inference, `loss` and `train_op` need to be `NULL`. Users need to early return the expected `estimator_spec`. 

```
custom_model_fn <- function(features, labels, mode, params, config) {
    # Create three fully connected layers respectively of size 10, 20, and 10 with
    # each layer having a dropout probability of 0.1.
    logits <- features %>%
      tf$contrib$layers$stack(
        tf$contrib$layers$fully_connected, c(10L, 20L, 10L),
        normalizer_fn = tf$contrib$layers$dropout,
        normalizer_params = list(keep_prob = 0.9)) %>%
      tf$contrib$layers$fully_connected(3L, activation_fn = NULL) # Compute logits (1 per class) and compute loss.

    predictions <- list(
      class = tf$argmax(logits, 1L),
      prob = tf$nn$softmax(logits))
    
    if(mode == "infer"){
      return(estimator_spec(predictions = predictions, mode = mode, loss = NULL, train_op = NULL))
    }
    
    labels <- tf$one_hot(labels, 3L)
    loss <- tf$losses$softmax_cross_entropy(labels, logits)
    
    # Create a tensor for training op.
    train_op <- tf$contrib$layers$optimize_loss(
      loss,
      tf$contrib$framework$get_global_step(),
      optimizer = 'Adagrad',
      learning_rate = 0.1)

    return(estimator_spec(predictions, loss, train_op, mode))
  }
```

title: Automatically map R objects to TF.Learn column variables
description:
When building a model with TF.Learn, one must generate 'column's from the input data, typically defining the 'type' or 'shape' of data expected in a particular column. For example, the example in https://www.tensorflow.org/tutorials/tflearn/ has:

```
# Specify that all features have real-value data
feature_columns = [tf.contrib.layers.real_valued_column("", dimension=4)]
```

indicating that the feature-columns input is an array with a single real valued column of dimension 4 (if I am understanding the API correctly). Other columns are described at https://www.tensorflow.org/tutorials/linear/overview.

We likely want to be able to construct this `feature_columns` object based on R inputs automatically. For example:

| R | TF.Learn |
| - | - |
| numeric | `real_valued_column` |
| integer | coerce to numeric + `real_valued_column` (?) |
| factor | `sparse_column_with_keys` |
| string | `sparse_column_with_hash_bucket` |

We may also want to make the transformations applied here user-configurable, e.g. with something like:

```
feature.transformations <- list(
    Petal.Length = function(x) {
        # transform the 'Petal.Length' column before passing to TF.Learn
    })
)
```

We might also want to just avoid making this part of the interface, and ask the user to explicitly transform the data before calling into the `tflearn` APIs -- I'm not yet sure what is most appropriate.

@terrytangyuan, does this sound like the right approach to you?
